{{short description|Rotor cipher machine}}
{{italic title|string=Schlüsselgerät}}
[[File:Hitlermühle IMG 1481.JPG|thumb|''Schlüsselgerät'' 41 at the [[Fort Reuenthal]] Museum]]
{{use dmy dates|date=July 2020}}
The '''''Schlüsselgerät'' 41''' ("Cipher Machine 41"), also known as the '''SG-41''' or '''Hitler mill''', was a [[rotor machine|rotor cipher machine]], first produced in 1941 in [[Nazi Germany]], that was designed as a potential successor for the [[Enigma machine]]. It saw limited use by the ''[[Abwehr]]'' (German Army intelligence) towards the end of [[World War II]].<ref name="NSA-German">{{cite web |url=https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/70/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/wwii/german_cipher.pdf |title=German Cipher Machines of World War II |pages=22–25 |work=Center for Cryptologic History |publisher=[[National Security Agency]] |accessdate=2 June 2019 |year=2014 }}</ref><ref name=heise>{{cite news |url=https://www.heise.de/tp/features/Hitlers-letzte-Maschinen-3435701.html |title=Hitlers letzte Maschinen |trans-title=Hitler's Last Machines |date=2 August 2004 |first=Klaus |last=Schmeh |work=[[Telepolis]] |publisher=[[Heinz Heise|Heise]] |accessdate=2 June 2019 }}</ref><ref name=jproc />

== History ==
[[File:Schlüsselgerät 41.jpg|thumb|An SG-41 ready to encipher text]]
The SG-41 was created under order of the ''[[Waffenamt|Heereswaffenamt]]'' ([[General der Nachrichtenaufklärung#Inspectorate 7/VI organisation|Inspectorate 7/VI organisation]])<ref name="Pröse">{{cite report |first=Michael |last=Pröse |title=Chiffriermaschinen und Entzifferungsgeräte im Zweiten Weltkrieg{{snd}}Technikgeschichte und informatikhistorische Aspekte |work=[[Technische Universität Chemnitz]] |date=December 2004 |pages=64–65 }}</ref> as a collaboration between German cryptographer [[Fritz Menzer]] and [[Wanderer (company)|Wanderer]], a leading typewriter manufacturer.<ref name="Batey">{{cite book |isbn=9781906447151 |first=Mavis |last=Batey |title=Dilly: The Man Who Broke Enigmas |publisher=Dialogue Books |page=212 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QF21AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA191|year=2017}}</ref> The machine also acquired the nickname "Hitler mill" because of the large crank attached to the side of the unit. Instead of using a lampboard like the Enigma, the SG-41 printed both the plaintext and ciphertext of the message onto two paper tapes. Due to wartime shortages of [[light metal]]s such as [[aluminium]] and [[magnesium]], the SG-41 weighed approximately {{convert|13.5|kg|lb}},<ref name="Pröse" /> which made it unsuitable for the front lines.<ref name="NSA-German" />

Menzer intended for the SG-41 to fully replace Enigma, which he considered to no longer be secure;<ref name=Pröse /> the ''[[Luftwaffe]]'' and ''[[German Army (1935–1945)|Heer]]'' ordered around 11,000 units.<ref name="Batey" />

A total of 1,000 units were produced. Various sources have reported production figures as low as 500 units due to [[materiel]] shortages,<ref name=jproc>{{cite web |url=http://www.jproc.ca/crypto/schluesselgeraet_41.html |website=jproc.ca |title=Schluesselgeraet SG-41 (Hitlermuehle) |accessdate=4 June 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |isbn=978-3868340440 |first=Klaus |last=Schmeh |title=Codeknacker gegen Codemacher. Die faszinierende Geschichte der Verschlüsselung Gebundenes |date=5 December 2014 |publisher=W3L-Verlag  |page=373 }}</ref> but production was halted after 1,000 units, as it was considered too heavy for use on the front. In December 1943, General [[Fritz Thiele]] ordered production to cease by the end of 1944.<ref name="Pröse" /> Beginning on 12 October 1944, the first deliveries to the ''[[Abwehr]]'' began.<ref name="cryptomuseum.com">{{cite web |url=https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/sg41/index.htm |title=Schlüsselgerät 41 |work=Crypto Museum |accessdate=2 June 2019 }}</ref> In the final months of the war, the SG-41 was used instead of the ''Abwehr'' Enigma.<ref name="NSA-German" />

== Function ==
[[File:Six Cipher Wheels of SG-41.jpg|thumb|The SG-41 had six cipher rotors.]]
[[File:Hitlermühle IMG 1481 excerpt.jpg|thumb|The "J" key was red and was used to switch between letters and numbers; "JRQJ" would represent "41".]]
Functionally, the machine had greater similarities with the [[Boris Hagelin]] [[M-209|C-Series]]. The SG-41 had six encryption rotors, compared to the Enigma, which had either three or four, in addition to a number of advanced features,<ref>Klaus Kopacz and Paul Reuvers, ''[https://www.cryptomuseum.com/pub/index.htm#cm_sg41 Schlüsselgerät 41 - Technical aspects of the German WWII Hitlermühle]''. Crypto Museum, 6 February 2010.[https://www.cryptomuseum.com/pub/index.htm#cm_sg41]</ref> making it much more resistant to cryptanalysis than the Enigma or other contemporary Hagelin machines.<ref>{{cite web |title=European Axis Signal Intelligence in World War II – Volume 2: Notes on German High Level Cryptography and Cryptanalysis |url=https://www.cryptomuseum.com/intel/nsa/files/volume_2.pdf |work=[[National Security Agency]] |page=29 |accessdate=3 June 2019 |date=1 May 1946 }}</ref> While the Enigma rotors advanced by one for each letter enciphered, the SG-41's wheels interacted with each other and moved irregularly. Similar functionality was not adopted in a mass-produced cipher machine until 1952 with the advent of the Hagelin [[CX-52]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ciphermachinesandcryptology.com/en/c52tech.htm |title=The Hagelin C-52 and CX-52 Cipher Machines |first=Dirk |last=Rijmenants |work=Cipher Machines And Cryptology |access-date=4 June 2019 }}</ref>

== Cryptanalysis ==
The Allied codebreakers in [[Bletchley Park]] considered the device a "mystery".<ref name="Batey" /> Only a handful of messages were able to be deciphered during the war, namely when two messages were "[[Cryptanalysis#Depth|in depth]]" i.e. encrypted with the same key. The inner workings of the device were unclear until after the war, so it was not possible to perform a systematic cryptanalysis on the messages. Allied codebreakers referred to it as a "remarkable machine".<ref name="cryptomuseum.com" />

== SG-41Z ==
In the final months of the war, an additional 550 units were built, which are referred to as the '''SG-41Z'''.<ref name="Pröse" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.deutsches-museum.de/forschung/forschungsbereiche/wissenschaftsgesch/digitale-kulturen/kryptografie/schluesselgeraet-sg41-z/ |lang=de |title=Das Schlüsselgerät SG41-Z von Fritz Menzer (1908-2005) |trans-title=The Cipher Machine 41-Z from Fritz Menzer (1908-2005) |work=[[Deutsches Museum]] |access-date=4 June 2019 |first=Carola |last=Dahlke |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180216183626/https://www.deutsches-museum.de/forschung/forschungsbereiche/wissenschaftsgesch/digitale-kulturen/kryptografie/schluesselgeraet-sg41-z/ |archive-date=16 February 2018 }}</ref> This model only allowed the numbers 0–9 to be enciphered and was used by the ''[[Luftwaffe]]'' for weather reports.<ref name="cryptomuseum.com" />

== Find near Aying ==
On 5 May 2017, two hobbyist [[treasure hunter]]s found an SG-41 using a metal detector in a forest near the [[Bavaria]]n city of [[Aying]], buried approximately {{convert|40|cm|in}} deep.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.br.de/nachrichten/oberbayern/inhalt/schatzsucher-finden-chiffriergeraet-hitlers-muehle-100.html |title=Schatzsucher finden Chiffriergerät 'Hitlermühle' |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170821120149/http://www.br.de/nachrichten/oberbayern/inhalt/schatzsucher-finden-chiffriergeraet-hitlers-muehle-100.html |archive-date=21 August 2017 |work=[[Bayerischer Rundfunk]] |date=18 August 2017 |accessdate=4 June 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> The hobbyists donated their find to the [[Deutsches Museum]] in Munich instead of selling it privately.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.sueddeutsche.de/muenchen/wertvolle-maschine-schatzsucher-finden-seltenes-exemplar-der-hitlermuehle-1.3631297 |title=Schatzsucher finden seltenes Exemplar der 'Hitlermühle' |lang=de |trans-title=Treasure Hunters Find Rare 'Hitler Mill' |work=[[Süddeutsche Zeitung]] |date=17 August 2017 |accessdate=4 June 2019 }}</ref> The museum intends to [[Conservation and restoration of cultural heritage|conserve]] it in its current condition and display it in a new permanent exhibit, ''Bild{{snd}}Schrift{{snd}}Codes''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://blog.deutsches-museum.de/2017/08/18/enigmas-nachfolger-entdeckt/ |title=Enigmas Nachfolger entdeckt |trans-title=Enigma's Successor Found |first=Gerrit |last=Faust |work=[[Deutsches Museum]] |lang=de |date=18 August 2017 |accessdate=9 July 2025 }}</ref>
